title: China Delivers World's First Sodium-Ion Mining Truck as Battery Race Heats Up
excerpt: A 15,000 km trial proves sodium batteries can power heavy trucks in extreme cold, while CATL and BYD pour billions into production — with big implications for India's energy transition.
body:
• China has delivered the world's first sodium-ion battery-powered mining truck, marking a milestone in the race to commercialise alternatives to lithium-ion batteries for heavy industry.
  • FAW Jiefang completed a seven-month, 15,000 km real-world trial of sodium-ion batteries in heavy trucks, with the 339 kWh pack retaining over 90% capacity at -40°C and achieving 8,000+ cycle life under fast charging.
  • CATL is investing $735 million to build 40 GWh of sodium-ion production capacity, while BYD claims a sodium battery with 10,000-cycle durability — signalling an industry-wide shift.
  • For India, which imports most of its lithium but has abundant sodium resources, the technology could accelerate domestic EV and energy storage manufacturing under the Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiative.

China has delivered what it claims is the world's first sodium-ion battery-powered electric mining truck, a milestone that underscores the country's accelerating push to develop commercially viable alternatives to lithium-ion technology. The development arrives as Chinese battery giants race to bring sodium-ion cells from laboratories to production lines — with potential implications for India's own energy transition ambitions.

From Lab to Mine Site

Chinese heavy truck manufacturer FAW Jiefang recently completed a systematic seven-month trial covering more than 15,000 kilometres, testing sodium-ion battery packs co-developed with battery supplier Zhongke Haina (HiNa Battery). The 339 kWh sodium-ion pack was subjected to continuous service operations in both extreme heat and cold, including temperatures as low as -40°C.

The results were striking: the battery retained more than 90% of usable capacity at -40°C, charged fully in 20-25 minutes, and demonstrated a cycle life exceeding 8,000 cycles under fast-charging conditions — far surpassing conventional industry benchmarks.

"Sodium-ion battery materials have a milder chemical system and outstanding thermal stability, perfectly matching the operational needs of commercial vehicles for high-frequency heavy loads, all-weather high intensity, and high safety standards."

— Zhongke Haina, official statement

Separately, HiNa Battery disclosed that sodium-powered heavy trucks demonstrated approximately 15% lower energy consumption per kilometre compared with lithium-ion equivalents, with deeper discharge capability enabling roughly 20% longer range under typical conditions.

The Industry Heavyweights Join the Race

The sodium-ion push extends well beyond FAW Jiefang. CATL, the world's largest battery manufacturer, has committed over $735 million to build a 40 GWh annual sodium-ion battery production facility in Fujian province. In late April, CATL secured a record 60 GWh sodium battery order for energy storage applications.

BYD has developed a sodium battery with a claimed cycle life of 10,000 cycles, while BAIC Group has unveiled sodium battery samples with energy density exceeding 170 Wh/kg. CATL and Changan have jointly unveiled a passenger vehicle model equipped with sodium-ion batteries, slated for market launch in mid-2026.

Meanwhile, China's autonomous electric mining fleet at the Huaneng Yimin mine in Inner Mongolia — 100 XCMG ZNK95 trucks powered by lithium-iron-phosphate batteries — has demonstrated that electric mining is commercially viable, saving an estimated 15,000 tonnes of diesel and 48,000 tonnes of CO₂ annually.

What This Means for India

The sodium-ion breakthrough carries particular significance for India, which imports the vast majority of its lithium and faces growing concerns about supply chain dependence on China. Sodium is roughly 1,000 times more abundant than lithium in the Earth's crust and can be extracted from seawater, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency.

Indian institutions are already investing in the technology. Researchers at Bengaluru's JNCASR have developed a NASICON-type sodium-ion battery capable of 80% charge in six minutes with over 3,000 cycle life. Reliance and KPIT are targeting sodium-ion applications for three-wheelers and light commercial vehicles.

HiNa Battery's general manager Li Shujun has predicted that sodium battery prices could reach parity with lithium batteries by 2027 or 2028, driven by rapidly falling sodium costs and rising lithium prices. If that timeline holds, India's vast salt reserves could become a strategic advantage in the global battery race, potentially slashing EV battery pack costs by up to 40% and reducing dependence on Chinese lithium supply chains.
